mn121:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī, in the Eastern Park, in the palace of Migāra’s Mother.
mn121:2.1: Then when it was evening, the venerable Ānanda rose from meditation, and he went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, he said to the Blessed One:
mn121:3.1: ‘Venerable sir, once the Blessed One was living among the Sakyans; there is a town of the Sakyans called Nāgaraka.
mn121:3.2: There, venerable sir, I heard and learned this in the Blessed One’s own presence:
mn121:3.3: “Now I abide much in voidness, Ānanda.”
mn121:3.4: Venerable sir, was this well heard by me, well apprehended, well attended to, well remembered?’
mn121:3.5: ‘Certainly, Ānanda, that was well heard by you, well apprehended, well attended to, well remembered.
mn121:3.6: As formerly, Ānanda, so now too I abide much in voidness.
mn121:4.1: ‘Just as, Ānanda, this palace of Migāra’s Mother is void of elephants, cattle, horses and mares, void of gold and silver, void of the foregathering of women and men, and there is present only this non-voidness, that is to say,
mn121:4.2: the single state dependent on the community of bhikkhus;
mn121:4.3: so too, Ānanda, without giving attention to perception of village, without giving attention to perception of man, a bhikkhu gives attention to the single state dependent on perception of forest.
mn121:4.4: His mind enters into that perception of forest and acquires confidence, steadiness, and decision.
mn121:4.6: “Disturbances that would be present dependent on perception of village are not present here, disturbances that would be present dependent on perception of man are not present here, and only this measure of disturbance is present, that is to say,
mn121:4.7: the single state dependent on perception of forest.”
mn121:4.8: He understands: “This field of perception is void of perception of village.” He understands: “This field of perception is void of perception of man.” “There is present only this non-voidness, that is to say,
mn121:4.9: the single state dependent on perception of forest.”
mn121:4.10: So he sees it as void of what is not there, but of what remains there he understands: “There is that still present here.”
mn121:4.11: This too has been for him, Ānanda, an alighting upon voidness that accords with what actually is, without perversion of meaning, and is pure.
mn121:5.1: ‘Again, Ānanda, without giving attention to perception of man, without giving attention to perception of forest, a bhikkhu gives attention to the single state dependent on perception of earth.
mn121:5.2: His mind enters into that perception of earth and acquires confidence, steadiness, and decision.
mn121:5.3: Just as though a bull’s hide were freed from folds by stretching it with a hundred pegs;
mn121:5.4: so too, Ānanda, without giving attention to all the ridges and hollows, the river ravines, the tracts of stumps and thorns, the rocky inequalities on this earth, a bhikkhu gives attention to the single state dependent on perception of earth.
mn121:5.5: His mind enters into that perception of earth and acquires confidence, steadiness, and decision.
mn121:5.7: “Disturbances that would be present dependent on perception of man are not present here, disturbances that would be present dependent on perception of forest are not present here, and only this measure of disturbance is present, that is to say,
mn121:5.8: the single state dependent on perception of earth.”
mn121:5.9: He understands: “This field of perception is void of perception of man.” He understands: “This field of perception is void of perception of forest.” “There is present only this non-voidness, that is to say,
mn121:5.10: the single state dependent on perception of earth.”
mn121:5.11: So he sees it as void of what is not there, but of what remains there he understands: “There is that still present here.”
mn121:5.12: This too has been for him, Ānanda, an alighting upon voidness that accords with what actually is, without perversion of meaning, and is pure.
mn121:6.1: ‘Again, Ānanda, without giving attention to perception of forest, without giving attention to perception of earth, a bhikkhu gives attention to the single state dependent on perception of the base consisting of infinite space.
mn121:6.2: His mind enters into that perception of the base consisting of infinite space and acquires confidence, steadiness, and decision.
mn121:6.4: “Disturbances that would be present dependent on perception of forest are not present here, disturbances that would be present dependent on perception of earth are not present here, and only this measure of disturbance is present, that is to say,
mn121:6.5: the single state dependent on perception of the base consisting of infinite space.”
mn121:6.6: He understands: “This field of perception is void of perception of forest.” He understands: “This field of perception is void of perception of earth.” “There is present only this non-voidness, that is to say,
mn121:6.7: the single state dependent on perception of the base consisting of infinite space.”
mn121:6.8: So he sees it as void of what is not there, but of what remains there he understands: “There is that still present here.”
mn121:6.9: This too has been for him, Ānanda, an alighting upon voidness that accords with what actually is, without perversion of meaning, and is pure.
mn121:7.1: ‘Again, Ānanda, without giving attention to perception of earth, without giving attention to perception of the base consisting of infinite space, a bhikkhu gives attention to the single state dependent on perception of the base consisting of infinite consciousness.
mn121:7.2: His mind enters into that perception of the base consisting of infinite consciousness and acquires confidence, steadiness, and decision.
mn121:7.4: “Disturbances that would be present dependent on perception of earth are not present here, disturbances that would be present dependent on perception of the base consisting of infinite space are not present here, and only this measure of disturbance is present, that is to say,
mn121:7.5: the single state dependent on perception of the base consisting of infinite consciousness.”
mn121:7.6: He understands: “This field of perception is void of perception of earth.” He understands: “This field of perception is void of perception of the base consisting of infinite space.” “There is present only this non-voidness, that is to say,
mn121:7.7: the single state dependent on perception of the base consisting of infinite consciousness.”
mn121:7.8: So he sees it as void of what is not there, but of what remains there he understands: “There is that still present here.”
mn121:7.9: This too has been for him, Ānanda, an alighting upon voidness that accords with what actually is, without perversion of meaning, and is pure.
mn121:8.1: ‘Again, Ānanda, without giving attention to perception of the base consisting of infinite space, without giving attention to perception of the base consisting of infinite consciousness, a bhikkhu gives attention to the single state dependent on perception of the base consisting of nothingness.
mn121:8.2: His mind enters into that perception of the base consisting of nothingness and acquires confidence, steadiness, and decision.
mn121:8.4: “Disturbances that would be present dependent on perception of the base consisting of infinite space are not present here, disturbances that would be present dependent on perception of the base consisting of infinite consciousness are not present here, and only this measure of disturbance is present, that is to say,
mn121:8.5: the single state dependent on perception of the base consisting of nothingness.”
mn121:8.6: He understands: “This field of perception is void of perception of the base consisting of infinite space.” He understands: “This field of perception is void of perception of the base consisting of infinite consciousness.” “There is present only this non-voidness, that is to say,
mn121:8.7: the single state dependent on perception of the base consisting of nothingness.”
mn121:8.8: So he sees it as void of what is not there, but of what remains there he understands: “There is that still present here.”
mn121:8.9: This too has been for him, Ānanda, an alighting upon voidness that accords with what actually is, without perversion of meaning, and is pure.
mn121:9.1: ‘Again, Ānanda, without giving attention to perception of the base consisting of infinite consciousness, without giving attention to perception of the base consisting of nothingness, a bhikkhu gives attention to the single state dependent on perception of the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
mn121:9.2: His mind enters into that perception of the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and acquires confidence, steadiness, and decision.
mn121:9.4: “Disturbances that would be present dependent on perception of the base consisting of infinite consciousness are not present here, disturbances that would be present dependent on perception of the base consisting of nothingness are not present here, and only this measure of disturbance is present, that is to say,
mn121:9.5: the single state dependent on perception of the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.”
mn121:9.6: He understands: “This field of perception is void of perception of the base consisting of infinite consciousness.” He understands: “This field of perception is void of perception of the base consisting of nothingness.” “There is present only this non-voidness, that is to say,
mn121:9.7: the single state dependent on perception of the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.”
mn121:9.8: So he sees it as void of what is not there, but of what remains there he understands: “There is that still present here.”
mn121:9.9: This too has been for him, Ānanda, an alighting upon voidness that accords with what actually is, without perversion of meaning, and is pure.
mn121:10.1: ‘Again, Ānanda, without giving attention to perception of the base consisting of nothingness, without giving attention to perception of the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, a bhikkhu gives attention to the single state, the signless concentration of mind.
mn121:10.2: His mind enters into that signless concentration of mind and acquires confidence, steadiness, and decision.
mn121:10.4: “Disturbances that would be present dependent on perception of the base consisting of nothingness are not present here, disturbances that would be present dependent on perception of the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are not present here, and only this measure of disturbance is present, that is to say,
mn121:10.5: that which has life as its condition dependent on the presence of this body with its six bases.”
mn121:10.6: He understands: “This field of perception is void of perception of the base consisting of nothingness.” He understands: “This field of perception is void of perception of the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.” “There is present only this non-voidness, that is to say,
mn121:10.7: that which has life as its condition dependent on the presence of this body with its six bases.”
mn121:10.8: So he sees it as void of what is not there, but of what remains there he understands: “There is that still present here.”
mn121:10.9: This too has been for him, Ānanda, an alighting upon voidness that accords with what actually is, without perversion of meaning, and is pure.
mn121:11.1: ‘Again, Ānanda, without giving attention to perception of the base consisting of nothingness, without giving attention to perception of the base consisting of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, a bhikkhu gives attention to the single state, the signless concentration of mind.
mn121:11.2: His mind enters into that signless concentration of mind and acquires confidence, steadiness, and decision.
mn121:11.4: “This signless concentration of mind is also conditioned and mentally produced.”
mn121:11.5: He understands: “Whatever is conditioned and mentally produced is impermanent and liable to cessation.”
mn121:11.6: When he knows and sees thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, his mind is liberated from the taint of being, his mind is liberated from the taint of ignorance.
mn121:11.7: When liberated, there comes the knowledge: “It is liberated.”
mn121:11.8: He understands: “Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived out, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.”
mn121:12.2: “Disturbances that would be present dependent on the taint of sensual desire are not present here, disturbances that would be present dependent on the taint of being are not present here, disturbances that would be present dependent on the taint of ignorance are not present here, and only this measure of disturbance is present, that is to say,
mn121:12.3: that which has life as its condition dependent on the presence of this body with its six bases.”
mn121:12.4: He understands: “This field of perception is void of the taint of sensual desire.” He understands: “This field of perception is void of the taint of being.” He understands: “This field of perception is void of the taint of ignorance.” “There is present only this non-voidness, that is to say,
mn121:12.5: that which has life as its condition dependent on the presence of this body with its six bases.”
mn121:12.6: So he sees it as void of what is not there, but of what remains there he understands: “There is that still present here.”
mn121:12.7: This too has been for him, Ānanda, an alighting upon voidness that accords with what actually is, without perversion of meaning, is pure, and is unsurpassed by any other.
mn121:13.1: ‘Whatever monks or divines in the past, Ānanda, entered upon and abided in a voidness that was pure and unsurpassed by any other, they all entered upon and abided in this very voidness that is pure and unsurpassed by any other.
mn121:13.2: Whatever monks or divines in the future, Ānanda, will enter upon and abide in a voidness that is pure and unsurpassed by any other, they will all enter upon and abide in this very voidness that is pure and unsurpassed by any other.
mn121:13.3: Whatever monks or divines at present, Ānanda, enter upon and abide in a voidness that is pure and unsurpassed by any other, they all enter upon and abide in this very voidness that is pure and unsurpassed by any other.
mn121:13.4: Therefore, Ānanda: “We will enter upon and abide in the voidness that is pure and unsurpassed by any other”—
mn121:13.5: thus should you train yourselves, Ānanda.’
mn121:13.6: This is what the Blessed One said.
mn121:13.7: The venerable Ānanda was satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.
